Zuoz
tswots
n. (village of the Upper Engadine in the Grisons; a commune which chose the Reformation by its own vote)
Romansh Zuoz, from Latin subtus or a related form meaning below or beneath; the village stands on a terrace above the Inn.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Zuoz is a village of the Upper Engadine, high on the Inn above Samedan, and it was the seat of the Planta family, the leading house of the valley. Its interest for the dictionary lies in how it became Reformed. Under the Ilanz articles of 1526 the religion of a Rhaetian commune was decided by the commune: the men of the place assembled, heard the question, and voted, and whichever way the vote went the minority had to live with it. The Engadine villages went over in the 1520s and 1530s one by one in this manner, Zuoz among them, with the altars taken out and the Mass discontinued by resolution of the assembly. It is an uncomfortable procedure to describe. A congregation's doctrine was settled by a show of hands among the heads of households, who were not necessarily converted men, and the result was binding. The dictionary enters Zuoz because the procedure states, in its crudest form, a problem the congregational principle has to answer: a church governed by its members is governed by whoever its members are, and the remedy is not to take the government away but to be careful whom the church receives.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a vote as an expression of will or preference; an assembly as a company collected together; and a majority as the greater number.

expand to see more

VOTE, n. [L. votum.] Suffrage; the expression of a wish, desire, will or preference, in regard to the decision of a question.

ASSEMBLY, n. A company of persons collected together in one place, usually for some common purpose.

MAJORITY, n. [Fr. majorite.] The greater number; more than half of any number or company.

MEMBER, n. A part of a body; one of the persons composing a society or community.

RESOLUTION, n. The determination of a mind upon a certain course; a formal determination of an assembly.

Modern Corruption

Upper Engadine commune which voted itself Reformed under the Ilanz articles, with the altars removed by resolution of the village assembly.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the confusion of the parish with the church. In the Rhaetian system the commune and the congregation were the same body: every household of the village belonged, and the religion was decided by the village assembly. That gave the valleys the Reformation, and it also meant that a church's doctrine rested on the votes of men who had never professed faith. The same confusion produced, in other countries, the national churches in which baptism and citizenship are one thing; the dictionary names it as an error however convenient its results.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the gathered church. “Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls” (Act 2:41) is the order—word received, then baptism, then addition to the body—and the body so gathered is what Scripture calls “the house of God, which is the church of the living God” (1Ti 3:15). A congregation of all the inhabitants is a parish; it becomes a church when its members are believers.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek cheirotoneo (G5500), to appoint by a show of hands; Greek ekklesia (G1577), the called-out assembly.

expand to see more

Greek cheirotoneo (G5500) — to appoint by stretching out the hand; “ordained them elders in every church”, Acts 14:23.

Greek ekklesia (G1577) — an assembly called out; “the church of the living God”, 1 Timothy 3:15.

Greek apodechomai (G588) — to receive gladly, to welcome; “they that gladly received his word”, Acts 2:41.

Greek prostithemi (G4369) — to add to; “there were added unto them”, Acts 2:41.

Greek didache (G1322) — teaching, doctrine; “by sound doctrine both to exhort”, Titus 1:9.

Usage

"“when they had ordained them elders in every church” (Act 14:23) — the commune assembly voting its own religion and its own pastor."

"“Then they that gladly received his word were baptized” (Act 2:41) — the order Scripture gives, and the parish system reverses."

"“the house of God, which is the church of the living God” (1Ti 3:15) — a parish becomes a church when its members are believers."
